abstract: At least one-quarter of our gene regulatory sequences are derived from transposable elements (TEs). Their rapid evolutionary turnover fuels the innovation of species-specific regulatory networks, yet their activity must be tightly controlled for the integrity of broader gene regulatory programs. Although this is in part achieved through heterochromatin-based repression, notably by KRAB domain-containing zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs) in tetrapods, the regulatory landscape of TEs remains to be fully characterized. Here, we discover that SCAN domain-containing zinc-finger proteins (SZFPs), which originally arose through capture of the sequence encoding a retroviral capsid by a KZFP gene, have expanded their gene repertoires and diversified their DNA recognition specificity in a lineage-specific manner across amniotes. Our comprehensive identification of human SZFP binding sites revealed that they bind regulatory elements derived from distinct TE subfamilies of matching evolutionary ages. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that SZFP binding sites are inaccessible nucleosome-associated chromatin without accompanying heterochromatin marks, H3K9me3 or H3K27me3, and resist opening by pioneer transcription factors such as SOX2 and POU5F1 (also known as OCT4) as well as SWI/SNF-mediated gain of an enhancer-associated chromatin state. These results unravel a rapidly evolving epigenetic machinery responsible for controlling lineage-specific TE-derived regulatory sequences in a heterochromatin-independent fashion.
